opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think the honest answer is that I was optimizing the wrong things. At the time I was an undergrad, and the way most of us approached research was: pick a model architecture, tweak something clever in it, run it on a benchmark, and hope the number goes up. With Transformers and NLP back then, I spent a lot of energy on small architectural ideas, a different attention variant, some structural trick, without really understanding what the bottleneck was.

What I understand now is that the bottleneck mostly wasn't the architecture. It was data and scale, and also the engineering infrastructure to iterate quickly. The models I was training were tiny, the datasets were small, and my experiment loop was slow and messy. So even if an idea was reasonable, the signal was buried in noise. You couldn't tell whether something failed because the idea was bad or because the training setup was bad. And honestly, a lot of the time it was the setup.

The second thing is that I didn't have good research taste yet. I didn't know how to ask, "If this works, does it matter?" Many of the directions I chose were incremental. Even a positive result wouldn't have changed much. The work that ended up mattering, in the field broadly, was people who took a simple idea and pushed it really hard with good engineering, rather than people adding complexity.

That's partly why I moved toward building infrastructure, things like Tianshou, the RL library, and later focusing on training systems. I realized that if your tools are fast and correct, you can actually run enough experiments to learn something. A lot of research progress is just being able to iterate ten times faster than you could before. So the failure taught me that good engineering isn't separate from good research. It's often the foundation of it.

r001.rationale: The response says the models and datasets were too small and that even a reasonable idea’s signal was buried, communicating that the research needed scale to succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the honest answer is that I didn't fail because the ideas were bad. I failed because I was working at the wrong scale and didn't realize it yet.

When I was doing that early work, the whole field was still in the mindset of clever architectural tricks. You'd tweak the attention mechanism, add some inductive bias, run on a single GPU or a small cluster, and hope for a point or two on a benchmark. And sometimes you'd get it, but it never generalized. The gains would evaporate the moment you changed the dataset or the task. I remember being genuinely confused by that, because the reasoning behind each modification seemed sound.

What I didn't understand was that the bottleneck wasn't the architecture. It was compute and data. The Transformer was already good enough. What it needed was to be fed orders of magnitude more than any of us were feeding it. Once the scaling results started coming out, it became obvious that all those months I spent on small models were essentially measuring noise. The signal that mattered only shows up when you cross certain thresholds, and nothing I had access to at the time came close.

The second thing, and this is more personal, is that I was optimizing for publishable novelty rather than for things actually working. Those are not the same objective. A paper rewards you for a new idea with a modest gain. An actual system rewards you for boring, careful engineering: data cleaning, tokenization, stable training, good infrastructure. I undervalued all of that. Later, when I moved more toward systems and reinforcement learning infrastructure, I saw how much of the real progress lives in that unglamorous layer.

So if I had to compress it: I was asking the right questions with the wrong resources, and I was measuring success with a metric that didn't correlate with what I actually cared about. It took me a while to see both of those clearly, but I don't regret the detour. It made me much more skeptical of small-scale results, and that skepticism has served me well.

r001.rationale: The response says the research questions were right but the available resources were insufficient, identifying compute and data as the bottleneck and explaining that progress required scaling by orders of magnitude.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think I was too focused on the model and not enough on understanding the problem. With Transformers and NLP, it’s easy to assume that a powerful architecture will lead to good results. But you still need a clear hypothesis, suitable data, and a way to tell whether your experiments are teaching you anything. I can’t point to one definitive cause, but that’s how I now think about those early failures: I needed to be more systematic about what I was testing and why.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the early failures to insufficient problem understanding and experimental rigor; it does not say success required the capacity to scale, even with a correct research direction.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think I was too focused on getting the model to work and not focused enough on understanding why it should work for the problem. When the results were poor, it was tempting to keep changing the architecture or tuning parameters. But a disappointing result alone doesn’t tell you whether the issue is the data, the implementation, or the underlying idea. The lesson for me is to start with a clear hypothesis, establish a reliable baseline, and design experiments that actually distinguish between those explanations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unclear hypotheses, baselines, and possible causes of poor results, but does not state that the research needed the capacity to scale—even if its direction was correct.
